name: Tokyo
tagline: Neon precision and quiet ritual in endless measure.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Sep, Oct and Nov
whenBlurb: Late March to early April for cherry blossom, and late October–November for autumn colour, are the two windows worth planning a year around. Skip Golden Week (late Apr–early May) and the August heat.

ourTake.lede: Tokyo rewards precision and punishes the scattershot, pick two or three neighbourhoods and go deep rather than sprinting across the map. Book the difficult tables the moment you have dates; the best counters seat eight and vanish months out. And spend at least one evening entirely off the tourist grid, in a six-seat basement bar in Golden Gai or a yokocho under the tracks, where no one is trying to sell you Tokyo.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a precise, endlessly layered city where three-Michelin dining, quiet temples and next-day fashion sit within a single afternoon.
ourTake.skipIf: You are after a slow beach reset or want a single unhurried base rather than a dense, fast-moving metropolis.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Bulgari Hotel Tokyo
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 15, highest in Japan)
items.description: Italian jewellery-house glamour suspended in the clouds above Tokyo Station, the city's most-lauded address of the moment.

items.name: Aman Tokyo
items.description: Aman's first city house, a washi-and-stone sanctuary poised above the financial district, silence six floors deep.

items.name: Janu Tokyo
items.description: Aman's warmer, more sociable sibling, eight restaurants and one of the city's largest wellness floors, in the new Azabudai quarter.

items.name: Palace Hotel Tokyo
items.description: A serene, family-owned house looking straight onto the Imperial Palace moat, old-Tokyo grace, quietly perfected.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Otemachi
items.description: The surest hands in the city, high over the Imperial gardens, home to Est and the celebrated Virtù bar.

items.name: The Peninsula Tokyo
items.description: A landmark corner facing the Imperial Palace and Hibiya Park, Peninsula polish, with the city's grandest lobby tea.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Tokyo
items.description: The highest rooms in the city, crowning Tokyo Midtown, the skyline unrolls beneath your window.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Tokyo
items.description: The group's quiet precision above old-merchant Nihonbashi, a house of light, art and view.

items.name: The Capitol Hotel Tokyu
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide Five-Star (2025, five consecutive years)
items.description: Shoji screens, natural wood and a garden pond beside Hie Shrine, a true urban oasis, run with rare grace.

items.name: Hoshinoya Tokyo
items.description: A modern ryokan stacked into a tower, you leave your shoes at the door and the city at the pavement.

items.name: The Okura Tokyo
items.description: Mid-century Japanese modernism, faithfully rebuilt, the lantern lobby is a design pilgrimage in its own right.

items.name: Andaz Tokyo Toranomon Hills
items.description: A design-led sky house atop Toranomon Hills, with one of the city's best rooftop bars and views to match.

items.name: Shangri-La Tokyo
items.description: Chandeliered Asian grandeur directly above Tokyo Station, glamour with the platform at your feet.

items.name: Fairmont Tokyo
items.description: Fairmont's Japan debut, high in the Blue Front Shibaura tower, with commanding views over Tokyo Bay.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Tokyo at Marunouchi
items.description: A small, jewel-like Four Seasons over the rail lines, and the address of three-Michelin-lauded Sézanne.

items.name: Park Hyatt Tokyo
items.description: The city's most cinematic hotel, the New York Grill and Bar on the 52nd floor, above the clouds.

items.name: The Prince Gallery Tokyo Kioicho, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: High-floor rooms with a glass-walled sky lobby, one of the great value skyline views in the city.

items.name: The Tokyo Station Hotel
items.description: A restored 1915 red-brick landmark inside the station itself, European classicism at the heart of Tokyo.

items.name: The Aoyama Grand Hotel
items.description: Retro-modern glamour in the fashion district, a design house for members who came to shop and be seen.

items.name: Bellustar Tokyo, A Pan Pacific Hotel
items.description: The top floors of Shinjuku's tallest tower, the neon city spread out far below.

items.name: The Prince Sakura Tower Tokyo, a Luxury Collection Hotel
items.description: A low-rise house set in a historic Japanese garden, cherry trees, teahouses and quiet, near Shinagawa.

items.name: Hotel New Otani Tokyo, Executive House Zen
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide Five-Star (2025, Executive House Zen)
items.description: A serene, service-led wing looking over a 400-year-old garden, the best of a storied Tokyo institution.

items.name: Conrad Tokyo
items.description: A crisp, contemporary tower with wide views over Hamarikyu Gardens and Tokyo Bay.

items.name: Grand Hyatt Tokyo
items.description: Warm, grown-up luxury in the heart of Roppongi Hills, dining and galleries on the doorstep.

items.name: The Tokyo EDITION, Toranomon
items.description: Kengo Kuma-designed calm with a forest lobby and a rooftop bar the city talks about.

items.name: The Tokyo EDITION, Ginza
items.description: EDITION's second Tokyo house, dropped into the middle of Ginza, greenery, glass and quiet cool.

items.name: Hotel Chinzanso Tokyo
items.description: A grand hotel in a famous camellia garden, waterfalls, a pagoda, and evening mist among the trees.

items.name: Trunk (Hotel) Yoyogi Park
items.description: A small Japanese-Danish house on the edge of an urban forest, design-forward and quietly green.

items.name: Hyatt Centric Ginza Tokyo
items.description: A smart, well-located Ginza house for members who want the address without the icon's price.

items.name: Keio Plaza Hotel Tokyo
items.description: A large, capable Shinjuku classic, dependable comfort with pools and plenty of dining.

items.name: Hilton Tokyo
items.description: A reliable, roomy Shinjuku tower, easy, central and generous for a family on the move.

items.name: The Strings by InterContinental Tokyo
items.description: A glass sky-lobby above Shinagawa station, quiet luxury with the bullet trains at your feet.

items.name: Cerulean Tower Tokyu Hotel
items.description: High-floor calm above the roar of Shibuya, the crossing below, the city beyond.

items.name: The Gate Hotel Asakusa Kaminarimon by Hulic
items.description: A rooftop terrace looking straight at Senso-ji and the Skytree, old Tokyo, from above.

items.name: K5
items.description: Swedish design and warm concrete in a converted 1920s bank, the city's most characterful boutique stay.

items.name: Hotel Ryumeikan Tokyo
items.description: A warm, well-run house blending Japanese hospitality with an unbeatable station-side address.

items.name: Senso-ji Temple & Nakamise-dori
items.description: Tokyo's oldest temple (645 AD); walk under the giant red Kaminarimon lantern, then the Nakamise craft-and-snack lane to the incense-wreathed main hall. Go at dawn or after 8pm for the empty, lantern-lit version.

items.name: Meiji Jingu Shrine
items.description: A vast, hushed forest of 100,000 donated trees around Emperor Meiji's shrine, five minutes from Harajuku's chaos. Sunday mornings you may catch a traditional Shinto wedding procession.

items.name: Zojo-ji Temple with Tokyo Tower
items.description: A grand Tokugawa-family temple framed perfectly against the orange Tokyo Tower behind it - the city's best temple-plus-tower photograph, and rows of tiny Jizo statues in the garden.

items.name: Nezu Shrine
items.description: A 1900-year-old shrine with a tunnel of vermilion torii gates (a serene, uncrowded alternative to Kyoto's Fushimi Inari) and an azalea garden that erupts in colour each April.

items.name: Gotokuji Temple (the beckoning-cat temple)
items.description: Reputed birthplace of the maneki-neko; hundreds of white waving-cat figures line the racks in a quiet suburban temple. A charming, offbeat stop children love.

items.name: teamLab Borderless, Azabudai Hills
items.description: The reborn 'borderless' digital-art world (reopened at Azabudai Hills in 2024 after leaving Odaiba) - rooms with no maps where artworks flow between spaces. Book timed tickets well ahead; your advisor can secure a quiet slot.

items.name: teamLab Planets TOKYO
items.description: The barefoot, wade-through-water immersive counterpart near Toyosu (extended through 2027) - you walk into knee-deep koi-projection water and mirrored infinity gardens. Wear rollable trousers; hugely popular, so pre-book.

items.name: Mori Art Museum & Tokyo City View
items.description: Ambitious contemporary shows on the 53rd floor, paired with a wraparound observation deck - culture and skyline in one ticket, open late into the evening.

items.name: Nezu Museum
items.description: Kengo Kuma's serene building of pre-modern Asian art, but the real draw is the hidden strolling garden of stone lanterns and teahouses - a green pause steps off luxury Omotesando.

items.name: Tokyo National Museum
items.description: Japan's oldest and largest museum; the Honkan gallery walks you through samurai armour, swords, ukiyo-e and ceramics in one graceful sweep. The place to grasp the whole arc of Japanese art.

items.name: Ghibli Museum, Mitaka
items.description: Miyazaki's whimsical museum with an exclusive short film, the Catbus and rooftop robot soldier. Strictly advance-reservation only (tickets released monthly and sell out in minutes) - have your advisor book the instant they open.

items.name: Ota Memorial Museum of Ukiyo-e Art
items.description: An intimate museum devoted entirely to woodblock prints - Hokusai, Hiroshige, Utamaro - with rotating themed shows. Small, uncrowded and deeply rewarding for a couple of quiet hours.

items.name: Shibuya Crossing & Hachiko
items.description: The world's busiest pedestrian scramble - thousands cross at once under the neon. Watch from the Starbucks window or Mag's Park rooftop, and greet the loyal-dog Hachiko statue nearby.

items.name: Shibuya Sky
items.description: An open-air rooftop deck 230m up with a glass-edge sky corner and hammocks - the most cinematic sunset-into-neon view in the city. Book the sunset slot ahead; it goes fast.

items.name: Tokyo Skytree
items.description: At 634m the tallest tower in Japan, with two glass observation decks over the endless grey sprawl to Mt. Fuji on clear days. The base holds the Solamachi mall and an aquarium for families.

items.name: Tokyo Tower
items.description: The 1958 Eiffel-inspired orange icon, still beloved and beautifully lit at night. Less about the view than the nostalgia; best admired from Zojo-ji or a nearby rooftop bar.

items.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building observatory
items.description: A free 202m observation deck in Kenzo Tange's twin-tower city hall - a smart no-cost skyline view, plus the nightly 'Tokyo Night & Light' projection show on the facade.

items.name: Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden
items.description: A vast garden blending French formal, English landscape and Japanese strolling styles - Tokyo's finest cherry-blossom lawn in spring and a serene escape from Shinjuku's density any season.

items.name: Rikugien Garden
items.description: An exquisite Edo-era strolling garden built around a central pond recreating scenes from classical poetry - autumn maple illuminations here are among the city's most beautiful evenings.

items.name: Hama-rikyu Gardens & tea house
items.description: A former shogun's seaside garden with a tidal pond, framed against Shiodome skyscrapers; take matcha and a wagashi sweet at the pond-island Nakajima teahouse. Arrive by the Sumida river boat.

items.name: Imperial Palace East Gardens
items.description: Free-to-enter grounds of the former Edo Castle - climb the old keep foundation for city views, wander the moats and stone walls at the literal centre of Tokyo.

items.name: Kiyosumi Teien Garden
items.description: A jewel-box strolling garden of stepping-stones across a koi pond and rare landscape rocks, in Tokyo's third-wave-coffee district - pair it with a flat white in a warehouse cafe nearby.

items.name: Ueno Park & its museums
items.description: A sprawling park holding the National Museum, Western Art museum, science museum, a zoo and Shinobazu lotus pond - the densest culture cluster in the city, glorious under cherry blossom.

items.name: Shibuya district wander
items.description: Beyond the crossing: the sleek Miyashita Park, the alleys of Nonbei Yokocho, and Shibuya's new towers. Youth-energy central, best explored on foot from late afternoon into the neon evening.

items.name: Shinjuku & Golden Gai / Omoide Yokocho
items.description: Neon canyons, the tiny-bar warren of Golden Gai and the smoky yakitori lane of Omoide Yokocho ('Memory Lane'). Atmospheric and cinematic; an advisor can pre-arrange a table in the good ones.

items.name: Harajuku - Takeshita & Cat Streets
items.description: Japan's youth-fashion crucible: candy-coloured Takeshita Street for the spectacle, quieter Cat Street and Ura-Harajuku backstreets for the actual good boutiques and coffee.

items.name: Ginza stroll
items.description: Tokyo's grand shopping boulevard of flagship maisons and department stores; on weekend afternoons the main avenue closes to traffic and becomes a 'pedestrian paradise'. Best paired with a depachika lunch.

items.name: Yanaka old-town wander
items.description: One of the few districts to survive the war and quakes - low wooden houses, artisan shops, a rambling cemetery of cherry trees and the shitamachi (old downtown) atmosphere Tokyo mostly lost.

items.name: Shimokitazawa
items.description: A low-rise, car-free maze of vintage shops, indie cafes, record stores and tiny theatres - Tokyo's bohemian heart, best on a slow weekend afternoon with no plan.

items.name: Kagurazaka
items.description: A former geisha quarter of cobbled slopes and hidden ryotei restaurants, with a French accent from its expat community - discreet, refined and lovely for an evening walk to dinner.

items.name: Nakameguro & the Meguro River
items.description: A canal lined with cherry trees, boutiques and the flagship Starbucks Reserve Roastery. Peak magic during sakura season when the river glows with lanterns; chic and calm the rest of the year.

items.name: Koenji
items.description: Retro, gritty and unpolished - vintage clothing, live-music dives and standing bars, plus the huge Awa-Odori dance festival in August. Real, un-touristed Tokyo counter-culture.

items.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
items.description: The inner wholesale market moved to Toyosu, but the outer market thrives - grazing stalls of tamago, uni, grilled scallops, knives and dashi. Go hungry by 9am; ask about veg-friendly stalls.

items.name: Toyosu Market tuna auction
items.description: The successor to Tsukiji's famous auction - watch the pre-dawn tuna bidding from a viewing deck (advance application for the ground-floor window), then eat the freshest sushi breakfast in Tokyo.

items.name: Ameyoko Market
items.description: A raucous open-air bazaar under the train tracks - seafood, spices, sneakers and cheap eats shouted from every stall. The closest Tokyo gets to a South-Asian-style street market, and fun with kids.

items.name: Depachika food hall grazing
items.description: The basement food halls of Isetan Shinjuku, Mitsukoshi Ginza or Takashimaya are gastronomic theatre - jewel-like sweets, pristine bento, tea and sake. A refined, air-conditioned way to taste Japan.

items.name: Grand Sumo tournament, Ryogoku Kokugikan
items.description: The Tokyo basho runs three times a year (January, May, September). Ringside box seats are electric; between tournaments an advisor can arrange a morning stable practice visit instead.

items.name: Kabuki matinee at Kabukiza
items.description: Japan's premier kabuki theatre - stylised drama, dazzling costumes and the hanamichi runway through the audience. English earphone guides make it accessible; single-act tickets suit a first taste.

items.name: Private tea ceremony
items.description: A guided chado ceremony - the choreographed whisking and serving of matcha in a tatami room - is one of Japan's most quietly moving experiences. Advisor arranges an English-speaking, private session.

items.name: Sake tasting & brewery visit
items.description: A guided flight through junmai, ginjo and daiginjo, or a small Tokyo-area kura (brewery) tour, decodes Japan's rice wine. Curated private tastings can be set up for members.

items.name: Onsen or design sento soak
items.description: Bathe in mineral waters - the theatrical Oedo-Onsen-style complexes, or beautifully restored neighbourhood sento. A restorative ritual; note tattoo policies, which an advisor can pre-check for you.

items.name: Omotesando architecture walk
items.description: A leafy 'Champs-Elysees' lined with flagship boutiques designed by the world's star architects - Prada by Herzog & de Meuron, Dior, Tod's. An open-air museum of contemporary architecture and luxury.

items.name: Ginza Six & Ginza shopping
items.description: The district's most ambitious mall, with rotating art installations, a rooftop garden and a hidden Noh theatre, anchoring a walk past Wako, Itoya stationery and every global maison flagship.

items.name: Akihabara Electric Town
items.description: The neon capital of anime, manga, gaming and gadgets - multi-storey arcades, retro-game shops and pop-culture excess. Sensory overload in the best way, and unmissable for teens.

items.name: Nakano Broadway
items.description: A wonderfully weird retro mall of collectible, vintage-toy, manga and watch shops - Akihabara's older, cultier cousin. A treasure hunt for serious collectors, minus the crowds.

items.name: Sumida River cruise
items.description: Glide from Asakusa past a dozen bridges to Hama-rikyu or futuristic Odaiba - including the manga-artist-designed Himiko 'spaceship' boat. A restful way to see the city change from old to new.

items.name: Todoroki Valley
items.description: A cool, green ravine walk along a stream, complete with a small temple and teahouse - startlingly rural for central Tokyo, and blissfully quiet. A secret local favourite for a hot day.

items.name: Kamakura day-trip
items.description: A seaside former capital of Zen temples, bamboo groves at Hokoku-ji and the open-air Great Buddha of Kotoku-in. Add the Enoshima tram along the coast for a perfect, unhurried day.

items.name: Nikko day-trip
items.description: The lavishly carved Toshogu shrine complex - the ornate opposite of Zen restraint - set among cedar forests, waterfalls and Lake Chuzenji in the mountains. A full, rewarding day north of the city.

items.name: Hakone day-trip
items.description: Hot-spring resort of ryokan, the Open-Air Museum's sculptures, a pirate-ship lake cruise and Fuji views from the ropeway over sulphur vents. Ideal as an overnight ryokan stay your advisor can book.

items.name: Mt. Fuji & Lake Kawaguchiko
items.description: The classic mirror-Fuji reflected in the lake, the Chureito Pagoda viewpoint and lakeside onsen. A private-car day-trip on a clear morning delivers Japan's defining image.

items.name: Yokohama day-trip
items.description: A breezy harbour city - Japan's largest Chinatown, the Minato Mirai waterfront, the Cup Noodles museum and Sankeien garden. An easy half-day that feels a world away from Tokyo's density.

items.name: Odaiba & the waterfront
items.description: A man-made bay island with a Rainbow Bridge skyline view, a Statue-of-Liberty replica, the giant Gundam robot, malls and hot-spring complexes. Family-friendly, and lovely at dusk.

items.name: Roppongi art triangle
items.description: The National Art Center's glass wave, the Suntory Museum's craft focus and Mori Art Museum form a walkable trio of world-class shows - the single densest hit of contemporary art in Tokyo.

items.name: Yoyogi Park
items.description: Tokyo's great democratic lawn beside Meiji Jingu - rockabilly dancers, picnics, drum circles and space to simply be. On weekends it becomes a free, joyful window into local Tokyo life.

items.name: Sézanne
items.description: Classical French rewritten with a light hand and Japanese ingredients, Tokyo's highest-ranked table in the world.

items.name: Narisawa
items.description: 'Satoyama' cooking that plates the Japanese landscape itself, forest, sea and soil, in sequence.

items.name: Florilège
items.description: Chef Hiroyasu Kawate's theatrical, sustainability-driven French, reborn in the new Azabudai quarter.

items.name: Den
items.description: The warmest kitchen in Tokyo, Zaiyu Hasegawa's playful, generous kaiseki, served with a grin.

items.name: Nihonryori RyuGin
items.description: Seiji Yamamoto's science-meets-tradition kaiseki, one of Japan's defining fine-dining rooms.

items.name: Kanda
items.description: Pure, unshowy kaiseki that has held three stars since the guide began, restraint as mastery.

items.name: Quintessence
items.description: No printed menu, complete trust, Shuzo Kishida's exacting French, unchanged in its pursuit of the perfect.

items.name: L'Effervescence
items.description: Shinobu Namae's nature-led French, quietly philosophical, deeply Japanese in spirit.

items.name: Sazenka
items.description: The only Chinese restaurant in Japan to hold three stars, Chinese technique read through a Japanese lens.

items.name: L'Osier
items.description: Shiseido's grand French salon in Ginza, old-world luxury, three stars, faultless service.

items.name: Joël Robuchon (Gastronomy)
items.description: The late master's flagship château, grand, gilded French dining that has held three stars from the start.

items.name: Kagurazaka Ishikawa
items.description: Intimate, seasonal kaiseki down a lantern-lit lane, three stars, and only a handful of seats.

items.name: Azabu Kadowaki
items.description: Playful, truffle-laced kaiseki from a chef who cooks exactly as he pleases, and holds three stars for it.

items.name: Kohaku
items.description: Koji Koizumi's refined, precise kaiseki, one of the quiet three-star greats.

items.name: Sushi Saito
items.description: Long held to be the finest sushi counter in Tokyo, and the hardest seat in the city to secure.

items.name: Maz
items.description: Virgilio Martínez's Peru-to-Japan altitude cooking, the Lima phenomenon, translated to Tokyo.

items.name: Crony
items.description: Modern, ingredient-led fine dining with a superb pairing programme, refined without ceremony.

items.name: Sukiyabashi Jiro Roppongi
items.description: The Jiro lineage, at the more reachable Roppongi counter, sushi as devotion.

items.name: Sushi Kanesaka
items.description: A benchmark Ginza edomae counter, classical, exact, and quietly warm.

items.name: Esquisse
items.description: Bright, delicate contemporary French high above Ginza, a room full of light and precision.

items.name: Akasaka Kikunoi
items.description: The Kyoto kaiseki dynasty's Tokyo house, seasonal Japanese cooking of great poise.

items.name: Ginza Koju
items.description: Understated, seasonal Ginza kaiseki from a chef's chef, quiet excellence, two stars.

items.name: Édition Koji Shimomura
items.description: Precise, seasonal French from a chef trained under the greats, measured and refined.

items.name: Ginza Shinohara
items.description: A Nagano-born chef's exacting kaiseki, the dashi alone is worth the journey.

items.name: Sugalabo
items.description: Yosuke Suga's membership-driven, no-menu counter, the city's most coveted contemporary table.

items.name: Tempura Kondo
items.description: The temple of vegetable tempura, feather-light, and unlike tempura anywhere else.

items.name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon
items.description: The counter concept that changed fine dining, small plates, open kitchen, red-and-black theatre.

items.name: Ryuzu
items.description: Generous, classical French with a warm room and famously fair value for the level.

items.name: Beige Alain Ducasse Tokyo
items.description: Ducasse's Chanel-topped Ginza salon, French cooking with a couturier's polish.

items.name: Ode
items.description: Yusuke Namai's contemporary French, inventive, personal and warmly run.

items.name: Tempura Motoyoshi
items.description: A serene tempura counter that climbed to two stars, course after course, impossibly light.

items.name: Nabeno-Ism
items.description: Riverside French from a Robuchon protégé, with the Skytree framed in the window.

items.name: Ristorante Aso
items.description: Refined, produce-led Italian in a leafy villa, one of Tokyo's most gracious Italian rooms.

items.name: Faro
items.description: Shiseido's rooftop Italian, plant-forward, seasonal and quietly progressive.

items.name: Ginza Kojyu
items.description: Seasonal Japanese cooking of quiet confidence, at the heart of Ginza.

items.name: Kabi
items.description: A young, Nordic-influenced kitchen and natural-wine list that quietly became a Tokyo favourite.

items.name: Bird Land
items.description: The yakitori counter that made grilled chicken a fine art, every part of the bird, perfectly charred.

items.name: Bar Benfiddich
items.description: A no-menu apothecary bar where the cocktails are built from herbs the bartender grows himself.

items.name: Nakajima
items.description: A one-star kitchen whose sardine lunches are among the great bargains in Tokyo dining.

items.name: Tonkatsu Narikura
items.description: Regarded by many as the finest tonkatsu in Japan, worth the trek out of the centre.

items.name: Tachiguisushi Sushikawa
items.description: Stand-up sushi of real quality, counter chat, top fish, none of the ceremony.

items.name: The Bellwood
items.description: A Taisho-era-styled bar reimagining kaiseki as cocktails, playful, precise, deeply Tokyo.

items.name: The SG Club
items.description: Shingo Gokan's genre-bending drinking den, 'Guzzle' below, 'Sip' above, both excellent.

items.name: Nakiryu
items.description: The tantanmen that put a ramen shop on the world's radar, worth every minute of the queue.

items.name: Japanese Soba Noodles Tsuta
items.description: The first ramen shop in the world to win a Michelin star, truffle-scented shoyu, still exceptional.

items.name: Ginza Kagari
items.description: A silky chicken-paitan ramen down a Ginza alley, the bowl that converts the sceptics.

items.name: Afuri
items.description: The yuzu-shio ramen that became a Tokyo signature, light, citrus-bright, endlessly copied.

items.name: Bar High Five
credentials: Former World's 50 Best Bars (No. 12) & Asia's 50 Best Bars top-tier
The benchmark of the Ginza cocktail tradition
items.description: Hidetsugu Ueno pours the definitive Ginza cocktail, no menu, no theatrics, just the finest classic in Tokyo.

items.name: New York Bar
credentials: The 'Lost in Translation' bar, 52nd floor of the Park Hyatt
items.description: The most cinematic bar in Tokyo, jazz, deep leather, and the Shinjuku skyline that fixed the city in the world's mind.

items.name: Star Bar Ginza
credentials: One of Ginza's most revered classic cocktail bars
items.description: Hisashi Kishi's temple of the classic, hand-carved ice, flawless technique, and the quiet of true Ginza mastery.

items.name: Bar Benfiddich
items.description: An apothecary in the sky, Hiroyasu Kayama builds each drink, no menu, from herbs and roots he grows himself.

items.name: The Bellwood
items.description: A Taishō-era drinking den reimagining kaiseki as cocktails, playful, precise and unmistakably Tokyo.

items.name: The SG Club
items.description: Shingo Gokan's genre-bending club, 'Guzzle' below for the crowd, 'Sip' above for the connoisseur, both superb.

items.name: Punch Room
items.description: EDITION's clubby ode to the punch bowl, retold through sake, yuzu and green tea, warm, low-lit, quietly glamorous.

items.name: Bar Libre
items.description: A serious, spirits-deep cocktail room from a celebrated bar group, classical technique, encyclopaedic backbar.

items.name: Gold Bar at EDITION
items.description: A gilded, curtained hideaway channelling pre-Prohibition America, opulent, intimate and out of sight of the street.

items.name: Tokyo Confidential
items.description: Caviar, champagne and mischievous cocktails with Tokyo Tower framed in the window, a sophisticated house party.

items.name: Gen Yamamoto
credentials: Regularly named among the world's most singular cocktail experiences
items.description: Eight seats, a seasonal tasting flight of cocktails built from the day's produce, the omakase of the bar world.

items.name: Bar Trench
credentials: A cornerstone of Tokyo's craft-cocktail movement
items.description: A tiny, absinthe-scented Ebisu original that helped write Tokyo's modern cocktail story, bohemian and beloved.

items.name: Bar Orchard Ginza
credentials: A Ginza original known for its fresh-fruit cocktails
items.description: A husband-and-wife counter where you choose a fruit and they compose the drink, inventive, warm, deeply personal.

items.name: Virtù
items.description: A jewel-box lounge high in the Four Seasons, French aperitifs, Japanese spirits, and the skyline through the glass.

items.name: The Aubrey
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars honouree (Park Hyatt Tokyo)
One of the city's most celebrated high-floor bars
items.description: A theatrical izakaya-bar on the 41st floor of the Park Hyatt, Eastern flavours, Western swagger, and the skyline entire.

items.name: Peter: The Bar
items.description: A silvery, sculptural room on the Peninsula's 24th floor, Hibiya Park and the Imperial gardens spread below.

items.name: Andaz Tavern & Rooftop Bar
credentials: MICHELIN Key hotel; among Tokyo's best-loved rooftop bars
items.description: The 52nd-floor terrace atop Toranomon Hills, one of the great open-air perches over the glittering city.

items.name: Golden Gai
credentials: An iconic surviving quarter of post-war Shinjuku nightlife
items.description: Six alleys of tiny post-war bars, each seating a handful, a warren of old Tokyo that never quite sleeps.

plan.heading: 4 days in Tokyo, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: From The Aman Tokyo atop Otemachi Tower, walk the Imperial Palace East Gardens in the morning calm.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Asakusa's Senso-ji and the Nakamise lane, then the craft ateliers of Kappabashi.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sushi at Sugita or Saito if the counter can be had; otherwise a faultless table at Aman's Musashi, then the 33rd-floor bar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Ginza before it fills, the Itoya stationery house, a private viewing of the Shiseido or Ginza galleries.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Nezu Museum's collection and its garden in Aoyama, unhurried, then coffee in the backstreets of Omotesando.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Tempura at Kondo or a kaiseki dinner at Ishikawa in Kagurazaka, a three-star of great restraint.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Toyosu market for an early tuna breakfast with a guide, then Hamarikyu Gardens and tea in the tidal-pond teahouse.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Meiji Shrine's forest, then the quiet luxury of Daikanyama, the T-Site bookshop and its lanes.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Yakitori omakase at Torishiki, then a nightcap at Bar High Five in Ginza, Hidetsugu Ueno's counter.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private tea ceremony and knife-forging visit, or a morning excursion to Kamakura's temples and great Buddha.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The teamLab Borderless installation in Azabudai, or a final wander through Nakameguro's canal.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Den, chef Zaiyu Hasegawa's playful, deeply Japanese tasting; drinks at Gen Yamamoto.

items.name: Marunouchi / Ginza
items.description: Polished, central and grown-up, flagship stores, the best hotels and Michelin density; for a refined, low-friction base.

items.name: Aoyama / Omotesandō
items.description: Architecture, quiet luxury boutiques and calm tree-lined streets, for design-minded travellers who want elegance over neon.

items.name: Shibuya
items.description: The pulse of the city, day and night, for younger travellers or repeat visitors who want to be in the thick of it.

events.name: Cherry blossom (sakura) season
events.note: A roughly ten-day window when the city's parks and canals bloom; the most beautiful and most contested time to visit.

events.name: Sanja Matsuri
events.note: Asakusa's wild three-day shrine festival, a hundred mikoshi carried through the streets, old Tokyo at full volume.

events.name: Sumida River Fireworks Festival
events.note: Around 20,000 fireworks over the river between Asakusa and the Skytree, the city's grandest summer night.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in Marunouchi, Ginza or Aoyama for polish and access; the best sushi counters and kaiseki rooms require booking weeks ahead, often through a hotel concierge, and quiet, understated dress and manners are the local grace.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Haneda (HND) for the shortest run into the city, or Narita (NRT); a pre-booked private car or hotel limousine is the calm way in, roughly 20-30 minutes from Haneda.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Tokyo's trains are impeccable and fast, but for discretion keep a private car and driver; the best neighbourhoods reward walking.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Ubigi, Airalo or a local IIJmio) gives instant nationwide coverage; wifi is everywhere and reliable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Japanese yen (JPY); cards and IC cards (Suica) are widely accepted, though keep cash for smaller restaurants and shrines, and there is no tipping in Japan.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Late March to early April for cherry blossom and November for crisp air and autumn colour are the two finest windows. Avoid June's rainy season through the hot, humid, typhoon-prone August; deep winter is dry but cold.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi in about 7-8 hours, and from Mumbai and Bengaluru, on Air India, ANA and Japan Airlines, mostly into Haneda (HND), the close-in, more convenient airport. ANA and JAL fly the 787 with excellent business cabins; choose Haneda over Narita to save an hour on the transfer into the city.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required or particularly recommended beyond routine; Japan is among the safest countries in the world, day or night. Tap water is clean and drinkable. No altitude concern.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Tokyo takes effort, traditional dashi (fish stock) hides in many dishes, so pure-veg and Jain travellers should lean on Indian restaurants, shojin-ryori (Buddhist temple cuisine, genuinely vegan) and the city's growing veg spots. Indian food is excellent and plentiful; Nirvanam and the shojin restaurant Bon are standout, refined options.
